feature: The shelf shows the component you just made
summary: Making a component now scrolls the Library shelf itself, so the tile it just made is on screen instead of sitting below the shelf's own little fold. A tile that was already showing does not move.
setup: Photonz Dev, Experiments window, release Next. Flags are on by default. The shelf's own fold only bites once there are more tiles than it can show, so step 2 shortens the shelf to get there faster.

try.do: Open a blank canvas and turn the shelf on with View then Show Library.
Drag the grab bar under the shelf up until only two rows of tiles show.
Draw two rectangles with R, marquee them with V, and press Command G.
Press Option Command K, type a name, press Return.
Repeat the last two steps until the shelf holds more tiles than its two rows.
Make one more component and watch the shelf: the new tile is on screen, on the bottom row.
Make one more straight after it, without touching the scroll.

evaluate: When the shelf scrolls, can you tell which tile is the one you just made?
Is scrolling to the bottom row the right landing spot, or would you rather the new tile came to the top?
Does the shelf moving under you feel helpful, or does it take away the row you were looking at?
The shelf and the dock can both scroll in the same beat. Does that read as one movement or two?
If you had a search typed in the shelf, the app clears it so your new component is not hidden. Is that right, or should the search win?
rough: The task assumed the shelf shows two rows at its default size; measured on the real app it shows three, so with a normal dock width the fold only bites at the tenth component. Shortening the shelf gets there in four.

Nothing marks the new tile as new. It is identified by its name, which only appears on the tile once you press Return on the Name field. A badge or a flash was deliberately not added: picking the tile would take the keyboard away from the Name field you are typing into.
The shelf lands the new tile flush with its bottom edge, which is the shortest move but leaves it right against the grab bar.
Verified with real window captures: the probe had Screen Recording granted, so both pictures here are the window as a person would see it.
